title: Grace opposed to nature: owed neither to merit nor to nature
source_text: IV. Et hoc sensu gratia opponitur naturae. Quoniam illa dona quae nobis supra naturam a Deo conferuntur, singulari quodam modo gratuita sunt: quia, scilicet, non tantum sub meritum personae non cadunt, sed neque naturae debentur. Quamvis enim Deus absolute nihil cuiquam debeat, neque ad quicquam obligetur, tamen ex hypothesi quod creaturam velit esse & operari, illi quodammodo ea praestare debet, sine quibus nec esse, nec operari potest.
pass_a_gloss: IV. And in this sense grace is opposed to nature. Because those gifts which are conferred on us by God above nature, are gratuitous in a certain singular manner: because, namely, not only do they not fall under the merit of the person, but neither are they owed to nature. For although God absolutely owes nothing to anyone, nor is obliged to anything, yet on the hypothesis that he wills a creature to be and to operate, he must in a manner furnish to it those things, without which it can neither be, nor operate.
pass_b_english: Thesis IV. In this sense grace is set against nature. The gifts God confers on us above nature are free in a special way: they do not fall under the person's merit, and they are not owed to nature either.

God, absolutely speaking, owes nothing to anyone and is bound to nothing. Yet once he wills that a creature should exist and act, he must in a way supply it with whatever it cannot exist or act without.

choices.why: A conditional debt: God owes nothing absolutely, but given his will to create he owes a creature what it needs to be and act.
